definition: A financial statement that summarizes a company's assets, liabilities, and owners' equity at a specific point in time, proving the fundamental accounting equation.
A report showing revenues earned and expenses incurred over a specific period, ultimately revealing the net income or net loss of the enterprise.
A financial report that details the cash inflows and outflows resulting from operating, investing, and financing activities during an accounting period.
A financial document explaining the changes in accumulated profits kept within the business from the beginning to the end of the reporting period.
The standardized collection of rules, conventions, and procedures that companies must follow when compiling their financial reports for external users.
The step-by-step sequential process of recording, classifying, and summarizing economic transactions during a specific period.
The initial step in the bookkeeping process where chronological entries of business transactions are recorded in a book of original entry.
The process of transferring transaction amounts from the general journal to the appropriate individual accounts within the general ledger.
An internal schedule prepared to verify that total debit balances equal total credit balances in the general ledger after all postings are complete.
Journal entries made at the end of an accounting period to assign revenues and expenses to the correct timeframe, adhering to the matching principle.
A method where revenues are recorded when earned and expenses are recorded when incurred, regardless of when cash actually changes hands.
A simpler bookkeeping approach where revenues and expenses are recognized only when cash is received or paid out.
Journal entries performed at the end of the fiscal year to reset temporary account balances to zero and transfer net income into retained earnings.
The systematic allocation of the cost of a tangible capital asset over its estimated useful economic life.
An expense calculation method that spreads an asset's cost evenly across every year of its expected useful life by subtracting salvage value.
A ledger account paired with and offsetting another account to reduce its reported book value on the financial statements.
A contra-asset account representing the estimated amount of accounts receivable that a company expects customers will fail to pay.
An inventory valuation method assuming that the oldest goods purchased are the first ones sold to customers.
An inventory cost flow assumption where the most recently acquired merchandise is treated as being sold first.
An inventory valuation technique that divides the total cost of goods available for sale by total units to determine a uniform cost per item.
A comprehensive financial plan detailing projected revenues, production costs, and overhead expenses for an upcoming fiscal period.
The overarching aggregate financial plan for an organization, combining all individual departmental and functional budgets into one cohesive document.
The quantitative investigation of the differences between budgeted figures and actual financial performance to identify operational inefficiencies.
A performance deviation where actual revenue exceeds budgeted revenue, or actual expenses are lower than projected costs, increasing net income.
A financial deviation where actual costs exceed budgeted amounts or actual revenues fall short of expectations, negatively impacting profits.
The formal planning process used by management to evaluate and select long-term investments in fixed assets like machinery or facilities.
A projected schedule of cash receipts and disbursements used by management to ensure adequate liquidity and prevent funding shortfalls.
A spending plan that adjusts automatically for changes in production volume or sales activity levels to provide a more accurate performance evaluation.
A financial planning method requiring managers to justify every proposed expenditure from scratch for each new period, rather than adjusting prior baselines.
The exact sales volume in units or dollars where total revenues precisely equal total fixed and variable costs, resulting in zero profit.
The amount remaining from sales revenue after subtracting all variable costs, available to cover fixed costs and generate profit.
Business expenses that do not fluctuate in total regardless of changes in production volume or sales levels within a relevant range.
Operating expenses that change in direct proportion to changes in the level of production or sales volume.
The monetary amount added to the cost price of merchandise to determine the final selling price that yields a profit.
The percentage of total sales revenue that remains after subtracting the direct cost of goods sold.
The fundamental financial concept stating that a specific amount of money is worth more today than the identical sum in the future due to its potential earning capacity.
The current worth of a future sum of money or stream of cash flows, discounted at a specific interest rate.
The projected value of an asset or cash investment at a specified date in the future, factoring in compound interest.
A financial statement evaluation technique that compares line items across multiple consecutive periods to identify growth trends and percentage changes.
A reporting review method where every line item on a financial statement is listed as a percentage of a base figure, such as total assets or total sales.
A liquidity metric calculated by dividing total current assets by total current liabilities to determine a firm's ability to pay short-term obligations.
A stringent liquidity test that measures a company's capacity to cover short-term debts using only its most liquid assets, excluding inventory.
A solvency metric comparing total liabilities to shareholders' equity to evaluate how aggressively a business is financing its growth through borrowing.
A profitability ratio that measures the net income generated relative to the total capital invested by the company's shareholders.
An activity metric showing how many times a company sells and replaces its stock of goods over a specific period.
The organizational policies, procedures, and safeguards implemented by management to protect assets, ensure accurate reporting, and prevent fraud.
The periodic process of matching the cash balance on a company's bank statement against the cash account ledger to identify discrepancies.
The independent examination of a company's accounting records and financial statements to verify fairness and compliance with established standards.
The direct expenses attributable to the production or acquisition of the merchandise sold by a company during a reporting period.
The cumulative total of net income that a company has reinvested in its operations rather than distributing to shareholders as dividends.
The systematic process a company uses to evaluate and select long-term investment projects or fixed asset purchases.
The difference between the present value of cash inflows and the present value of cash outflows over a specific period, used to determine project profitability.
The discount rate that makes the net present value of all cash flows from a particular project equal to zero.
The average rate of return a company is expected to pay to all its security holders, weighted by the relative proportion of each financing source.
The amount of cash generated by a company's normal, ongoing business operations.
The cash left over after a company pays for its operating expenses and capital expenditures, available for dividends, debt repayment, or expansion.
The strategy focused on maintaining efficient levels of current assets and current liabilities to ensure smooth day-to-day operations.
The time it takes for a company to convert its investments in inventory and other resources into cash inflows from sales.
The ideal order size that a company should purchase to minimize total inventory holding and ordering costs.
The temporary delay between the time a payment is initiated and when the funds are actually cleared and available in the recipient's account.
A bank-operated service that receives customer payments directly, speeding up collection times and reducing internal processing float.
The particular combination of debt, equity, and other securities that a firm uses to finance its overall operations and growth.
The degree to which a company uses borrowed money to finance its assets and amplify potential shareholder returns.
A multiple that measures how a percentage change in sales revenue impacts a company's earnings before interest and taxes.
A metric showing the sensitivity of a company's earnings per share to fluctuations in its operating income resulting from debt usage.
A foundational proposition suggesting that under certain market conditions, the market value of a firm is unaffected by its capital structure.
The proportion of net income distributed to shareholders in the form of cash dividends.
A policy where dividends are paid only after all profitable capital budgeting projects have been fully funded.
A corporate action where a company buys back its own shares from the marketplace to reduce outstanding supply and boost per-share metrics.
The practice of comparing financial statement data across multiple consecutive periods to spot growth trends and direction.
A technique where each line item on a financial statement is listed as a percentage of a base figure, such as total revenue or total assets.
A framework that breaks down return on equity into profitability, asset efficiency, and financial leverage components.
